trickyParts: The app Deployment's name, namespace and selector are the only fields whose change would make the consuming stack's preview a replacement rather than an update. They are unchanged and pinned by a test; the reviewer should treat any future edit to them as a breaking change to the consumer.

Recreate at one replica is not a conservative default, it is the only safe strategy there: a surged second envoy-dispatch cannot bind the exclusive delivery push durable while the old pod holds it, and a terminating pod stops being counted by the ReplicaSet controller, so maxUnavailable:1/maxSurge:0 does not avoid the overlap either.

The front door and the listener are recreated at every update whatever the app's replica count, so Serve is briefly down when the tailnet pod is replaced even at replicas: 3. A rolling update of the app alone is what this issue makes gapless; a front-door image change is still a short outage, and the README says so.

The Serve configuration now names the app's Service, which is the one claim in the design with no in-repo proof: TS_USERSPACE=true leaves the pod's cluster DNS alone, so tailscaled should dial <h>.<ns>.svc.cluster.local as an ordinary outbound connection. The first curl through the tailnet after the consuming stack applies is what confirms it.

The listener moved out of the app pod, so it binds 0.0.0.0 and cmd/listener/apiauth.go then refuses to start without a bearer. That is why this change generates a token and gives the same value to envoy-dispatch as ENVOY_TOKEN; a reviewer removing the Secret would make the listener refuse to boot, not merely lose authentication.
deviations: The plan named DependsOn for the app Deployment alone. The simplify pass's efficiency reviewer found that the listener dials the same SOCKS5 proxy and that envoy-listener exits on a failed initial NATS connect (cmd/listener/main.go), so on a fresh create it would crash-loop into Kubernetes' backoff while the update waits out its rollout. The listener now takes the same dependency, with its own assertion.

The plan's task 12 included a dispatch ask to the project owner to run the consuming stack's pulumi preview. The architect ruled at 21:05Z that this preview is INFRA-63's, which runs it in the repository where the stack lives immediately before its apply, and told this implementer not to open the ask; what INFRA-62 owes instead is the object inventory above, which is this handoff's objectInventory.

The plan rendered no lifecycle hook. Review round 1 added one: the app's envoy-dispatch container waits five seconds before it is signalled, because EndpointSlice removal is asynchronous while the server closes its listener on SIGTERM. The architect decided between the reviewer's two options (add the delay, or document the residual) and chose the delay, so that a request lost during INFRA-63's measured release does not cost a pull request here, a pin bump, a regenerated SDK and a second apply to measure again.

An earlier write of this handoff and of the pull request's body cited f8ec21dfc7245cd25eec7a9ee24c6b05b1aa0d46 as review round 1's code head. That is not a commit — GitHub answers 422 for it and `jj log -r` does not resolve it; it shares its prefix with the real commit, f8ec21dfc724e27e1b75c84ba4ff763902708436, and was wrong in its tail because the tail was typed rather than read. Both artefacts were corrected and say so in their own text, and every 40-character id in each is now checked against `jj log -r <id>` before it is posted. The wrong id survives deliberately in one place, the pull request body's correction paragraph, where it is the subject: a later tidy-up that 'fixes' it there destroys the record.

The plan rendered no guard across the module boundary. Review round 2 added one: packages/envoy/cmd/dispatch/pod_grace_period_test.go reads stopGrace and the rendered pod's golden, so raising stopGrace alone now fails a test in the lane its editor runs. The reviewer offered that or an exported constant both modules derive from, and sized the test as the smaller; it costs no exported API and no module surgery.
openQuestions: The front door's tailscale container keeps the sidecar's 100m CPU / 128Mi, with requests equal to limits. It is now a single-replica Deployment whose userspace SOCKS5 proxy carries every app replica's NATS traffic as well as all tailnet HTTPS, SSE and websocket traffic, and it cannot scale out by design. Nothing measured says 100m is too little, and raising it would change the pod golden, so this change leaves it as it was; INFRA-63's apply is the first run that can measure it, and the number may need raising with the replica count.

The envoy-dispatch server is still not safe at two concurrent processes (exclusive delivery durables, a per-process SSE broker and document rooms, an outbox publisher that claims no row, and loops written for one process). The component ships the capability with the default at 1 and the README says so; a sibling issue must land before INFRA-63 sets more than one replica in production.
discoveredComplexity: No surface in a Legion pod reaches a live cluster or the consuming stack: there is no pulumi state access (HTTP 403 on the state bucket), no gcloud, no Docker and no cluster credential. The production-like surface available for a Pulumi component is its own plugin binary driven through the Construct RPC server and read by the real Pulumi CLI, which is what the proof above uses; the deployed rendering is proved by INFRA-63.

The module's test suite has two environment-dependent failures in any pod without e2fsprogs (TestTheDataDiskIsFormattedOnlyWhenItReadsAsZerosToItsEnd and TestARefusedDataDiskIsNeverFormattedOnALaterBoot, both `these tests need mkfs.ext4 on this machine`). They fail on the base commit too and are green in CI's envoy-infra-go job.
